facts: The bonnacon (also bonasus or bonacho) is a legendary bull with inward-curving horns and a horse-like mane.
Medieval bestiaries usually depict its fur as reddish-brown or black.
Because the horns were useless for defense, it was said to expel caustic feces that burned pursuers so it could escape.

sources.title: Bonnacon
sources.supports: All three facts are in the lead of the article.

facts: A banshee is a female spirit who heralds a family death by screaming, wailing, shrieking, or keening.
The name is Modern Irish bean sí, from Old Irish ben síde, 'woman of the fairy mound' or 'fairy woman', tied to the síde burial mounds.

facts: The Tarasque is a creature of French legend. The Golden Legend describes a lion-like head, a turtle-like shell, six feet with bear claws, a serpent tail, and poisonous breath.
Tradition has St Martha confronting it while it swallowed a person, which became a stock image of the monster with a victim's legs still sticking out.
From 1474 René of Anjou used a tarasque figure in Tarascon's Pentecost festival; the festival continues.

sources.title: Tarasque

facts: Britannica: Baba Yaga, also spelled Baba Jaga, is an ogress in Slavic folklore who steals, cooks, and eats her victims, usually children.

She is a guardian of the fountains of the water of life. She lives with two or three sisters, all called Baba Yaga, in a forest hut that spins continually on birds' legs. The fence is topped with human skulls.
She rides through the air in an iron kettle, or in a mortar she drives with a pestle, and raises tempests as she goes. She often accompanies Death and devours newly released souls.

sources.title: Baba Yaga - Britannica Scholars
sources.supports: The spinning hut on bird legs, the mortar and pestle, the skull fence, the water of life, and the child-eating ogress role.

facts: The British Museum's schools guide says Ammit was not considered a goddess but a powerful and terrifying creature.
She is often depicted with the head of a crocodile, the forelegs of a lion, and the hind legs of a hippopotamus.

Her name means 'the devourer.' She devoured the hearts of the dead if they were unworthy when the heart was weighed against the feather of truth. She waited by the scales in the underworld, and her image in funeral art warned the dead to live well.

sources.title: Ancient Egyptian gods and goddesses | British Museum
sources.supports: Not a goddess; crocodile, lion, and hippopotamus body; devourer of unworthy hearts beside the scales.

facts: The Minotaur was a bull-headed monster born to Queen Pasiphae of Crete, lived in the maze-like labyrinth, received regular offerings for its hunger, and was slain by Theseus.
Theoi gives his proper name as Asterion, 'the starry one,' and says that name suggests a link with the constellation Taurus.

A classical encyclopedia summary preserved on the same page says he had a human body and a bull's head, or in other accounts the body of an ox and a human head; he was the offspring of Pasiphae and the bull sent from the sea, was shut in the Cnossian labyrinth, and Athenians were sent to Minos as tribute at fixed times.

sources.title: MINOTAUR (Minotauros) - Theoi Greek Mythology
sources.supports: Birth, labyrinth, hunger-offerings, death at Theseus's hands, the name Asterion, and the human-body/bull-head description.

facts: In Dungeons & Dragons the mimic is a monster that changes shape to look like an inanimate object, commonly a chest. It was introduced in the original Monster Manual (1977) and is described there as a subterranean creature that cannot stand sunlight and can mimic stone or wood, posing as stonework, doors, or chests.
The same article describes a powerful adhesive and pseudopods. Those two mechanics are specific to this game monster and are not used in the parody.

sources.title: Mimic (Dungeons & Dragons)

facts: Slimes are a fictional species of slime monster in the Dragon Quest series, conceived as a weak and common enemy for the 1986 game and inspired by Wizardry.

Yuji Horii said the slime was originally conceived as a pile of goo. Akira Toriyama's design came back as a teardrop, which the team considered perfect, and that teardrop became the series mascot and merchandise.

facts: The kappa, 'river-child', is a major Japanese water yōkai living in ponds and rivers, also called kawatarō in some places.
Older accounts make them drowners of people, horses, and cattle. Later tales have a captured kappa, sometimes with an arm pulled off, repay forgiveness with labor or a secret medicine.

They are pictured as green, slimy or scaly, webbed, and turtle-shelled. A dish (sara) of water on the head is their strength; spill it and they weaken. They like cucumbers and sumo, and are accused of pulling out a mythical organ called the shirikodama.

sources.title: Kappa (folklore)
sources.supports: River monster; head-dish; cucumbers; sumo; shift from killer to indebted helper.

creative.comedyConcept: Absurd comedy: a lifeguard whose authority is a bowl balanced on the head, stationed where the rain only falls on the plants. It blows the whistle at the weather.

The bake-danuki article says that in some regions tanuki are reputed to share kitsune-like powers of shapeshifting and possession. The noppera-bō article lists kitsune among shapeshifters who may stage a faceless scare.

facts: An oni is a yōkai, demon, or ogre in Japanese folklore, said to live in caves, deep mountains, or hell.

They are hugely strong, tied to thunder and lightning, and storied as murderous and cannibal. Typical pictures show horns, huge teeth, sometimes a third eye, red blue black or yellow skin, a tiger-skin loincloth, and an iron kanabō.

They can change shape to win trust. Heian setsuwa show them eating a person in one bite (onihitokuchi). They have also been linked to good fortune. Shuten-dōji is regarded as the most famous and strongest oni.

sources.title: Oni
sources.supports: Horned club-wielding ogre; shapeshifting; Heian man-eating tales; also a luck association.

creative.weaknessConcept: Anyone who is exactly on time. The stamp has nothing to say, and the club droops.
creative.loreSummary: Hornstamp took a chair in the Basement of Retired Bosses and kept the club. The club now clocks people in. Good fortune, for it, is a meeting that ends. It is a tower guardian pose, not a named legend and not a doctrine.

towerEnvironment.note: PROPOSED biome, not a previous game's canon.

creative.artworkPromptConcept: Comedy-fantasy basement, folding chairs, a throne used as a coat rack. A large ink-blue horned figure with a date-stamp for a club and a lanyard, mid-stamp. No tiger pelt, no feast, no specific manga oni.
creative.creativeBoundary: Does not use the man-eating stories or Shuten-dōji. Skin is one of the colors the article lists, chosen so the design is not only the red default.

entries.ipSimilarityReason: Oni are a folklore type. The office stamp, lanyard, and ink-blue hide avoid a specific anime costume and the tiger-pelt club portrait. Horns plus a heavy implement remain the tell.

research.origin: Japanese fantasy and science-fiction genre (anime, manga, light novels)
facts: Isekai (異世界, 'another world') is a Japanese fantasy and science-fiction subgenre about a person who is transported to another world and has to survive there, usually gaining formidable powers or importance they did not have before.

The crossing may happen through death and reincarnation, or through summoning by an object, god, or person. A common setting is a medieval fantasy world populated with humans, humanoids, and monsters.

The Wikipedia article traces the idea to older tales such as Urashima Tarō and to Western fantasy, and names Haruka Takachiho's novel Warrior from Another World and the anime Aura Battler Dunbine as early modern works, with The Twelve Kingdoms and Sword Art Online among the works that helped popularize the genre.

sources.title: Isekai
sources.supports: Definition, reincarnation or summoning, medieval monster-world setting, and the named early and popularizing works.

creative.visualIdentity: A short traveler's cloak over a body that is only a smudged badge photo, holding a prophecy scroll that stays blank. No spiky hair, no signature sword, no vehicle, no slime. The lobby desk is the whole battlefield.
creative.personality: Chosen, impatient, and stuck at the sign-in line.
creative.signatureTrait: The prophecy will not start until the log has a signature.
creative.comedyConcept: Satirical fantasy: another-world importance is real, and the visitor log is more real. No series hero is being quoted or costumed.

element.name: Echo
element.note: A story-shape that arrived wrong. Not a definition of the player's hybrid avatar, and not a reincarnation rite.

creative.signatureAbilityConcept: It will not swing until someone signs. A wrong name makes it chase the name on the line instead of the person in front of it.
creative.weaknessConcept: A signature that matches the badge. The scroll stays blank, and it has to admit it is merely early.
creative.loreSummary: Something was summoned into the Lobby of Lost Badges and gained a destiny it did not have at home. The desk asked it to sign first. Signfirst is not a player avatar and not a protagonist from a book or a show.

towerEnvironment.note: PROPOSED biome. Shares the lobby with Claimbite.

creative.artworkPromptConcept: Comedy-fantasy lobby desk. A small original cloaked arrival with a smudged badge for a face and a blank scroll, pen offered. Velvet rope, heap of badges. No recognizable anime hero, no vehicle, no magical sword.
creative.creativeBoundary: Does not name or costume any series listed in the research facts. Does not depict death-and-rebirth as a mechanic.

entries.ipSimilarityReason: Isekai is a genre full of copyrighted protagonists. Signfirst has none of their hair, weapons, or vehicles; the joke is the sign-in sheet. Medium because 'summoned and suddenly important' is the genre's whole plot.

facts: Tokusatsu (特撮, 'special filming') is the Japanese term for live-action films and television that rely heavily on practical special effects. The article credits Eiji Tsuburaya and says the word's modern media use was popularized around the first monster boom of 1966–1968.

It lists subgenres: kaiju such as Godzilla and Gamera, superheroes such as Kamen Rider, kyodai heroes such as Ultraman, and mecha such as Giant Robo. Some shows, including Super Sentai, combine several.

Suitmation is the technique of playing a monster with an actor in a costume, usually combined with miniatures and scaled city sets. The article says Tsuburaya developed this approach for the 1954 Godzilla, inspired in part by King Kong.

sources.title: Tokusatsu
sources.supports: Practical-effects genre, the listed subgenres, and suitmation as a costumed actor plus miniatures.

creative.visualIdentity: A person-sized original beast suit, somewhere between a bird and a teapot, magnificent until the shoulder. One zipper is stuck. A normal elbow shows. Not a rider helmet, not a giant reptile, not a silver giant, not a miniature city.
creative.personality: Heroic, muffled, and unable to start until the costume sits right.
creative.signatureTrait: The monster is a suit, and the suit is not finished.
creative.comedyConcept: Dark fantasy comedy: the shape is frightening in the doorway, and then the elbow is a person. The joke is affectionate toward a filming technique, not toward the audience.

element.name: Strike
element.note: The pose is the commitment that cannot start. No series color and no faction.

creative.signatureAbilityConcept: It strikes a tremendous pose and cannot take the step. Everyone waits on the zipper.
creative.weaknessConcept: Someone zips it. The suit becomes an ordinary impressive costume, the person inside apologizes, and they sit down.
creative.loreSummary: The Menagerie of Unfiled Beasts needed a monster and hired a suit. Zipperhide is the whole job. It is a guardian pose with nobody's franchise inside it.

towerEnvironment.name: The Menagerie of Unfiled Beasts
towerEnvironment.note: PROPOSED biome. Shares the menagerie with Curlhorn.

creative.artworkPromptConcept: Comedy-fantasy menagerie cage. An original bird-teapot monster suit, person-sized, one stuck zipper and a visible human elbow, straw on the floor. No tokusatsu helmet, no giant-monster silhouette, no miniature skyline.
creative.creativeBoundary: The research names several copyrighted series as examples of the genre. None of their suits, belts, or roars are used.

entries.ipSimilarityReason: Suitmation is a technique. The suit is an original bird-teapot with a stuck zipper, not Godzilla, not a rider, not a sentai monster, and not Ultraman. The elbow is the distance.

research.origin: Maritime legend, likely Dutch Golden Age, oldest known print version late 18th century
facts: The Flying Dutchman (De Vliegende Hollander) is a legendary ghost ship said never to be able to make port, doomed to sail forever. The article says the stories likely grew from the 17th-century Dutch East India Company era, and that the oldest known extant version is from the late 18th century.

If hailed, the crew may try to send messages to land or to people long dead. Nineteenth- and twentieth-century sighting reports described a ghostly glow. In sailors' lore the sight is a portent of doom. It was commonly imagined as a fluyt, a 17th-century cargo ship.
The first known print reference cited in the article is John MacDonald's 1790 Travels in various parts of Europe, Asia and Africa, in which sailors in a storm say they saw the Flying Dutchman.

sources.title: Flying Dutchman
sources.supports: The never-make-port ghost ship, the message-to-the-dead motif, the doom portent, and the 1790 print source.

creative.visualIdentity: A small fluyt-like cargo ship of fog and lobby velvet, lantern lit, stuck half through a doorway as if the throne landing were a harbor. Letters in bottles addressed to people who are already in the room. No barnacled face, no film captain, no cursed crew portrait.
creative.personality: Doomed to arrive, endlessly about to, and very concerned about the mail.
creative.signatureTrait: The dock is always the next one.
creative.comedyConcept: Epic but ridiculous: a portent of doom whose actual problem is parking. The ship fills the landing the way a boss would, and then it asks someone to take a letter.

element.name: Arcane
element.note: The unaccepted letter is the trick. Not a summoning rite and not a damage element. Looking like a legend stays the origin, not this tag.

creative.signatureAbilityConcept: It hails from the doorway and will not clear the lane until someone accepts the letter. Refusing the mail keeps the ship exactly where it is.
creative.weaknessConcept: Accept the letter and point at a pier that is only a chalk mark. It tries to dock, bumps the frame, and the grandeur leaks out as fog.
creative.loreSummary: Stilldock mistook the Throne Landing of Maybe for a harbor and has been about to arrive ever since. Seeing it is inconvenient. It is not a curse with a rule, and it is not the final floor, which the tower has not declared.

towerEnvironment.name: The Throne Landing of Maybe
towerEnvironment.note: PROPOSED set-piece color. OPEN-07: there is no locked last floor. This elite is not a world boss.

creative.artworkPromptConcept: Comedy-fantasy doorway that is also a stage. A small original 17th-century cargo ship of fog and velvet, half through the door, lantern and a bottle-letter. Empty throne with a maybe-not sign in the background. No film ghost captain, no barnacle face, no skull crew.
creative.creativeBoundary: Does not copy the Pirates of the Caribbean ghost ship or captain. The fluyt silhouette and the undelivered message are the sourced tells.

entries.ipSimilarityReason: The never-make-port ghost ship is public-domain maritime legend. The card is a velvet cargo ship stuck in a doorway with a letter, not a film's barnacled captain.
